summary: Updates the ACE DTLS profile of RFC 9202 to state that it applies to TLS as well as DTLS, for constrained environments.

plainLanguage.summary: A security recipe for small devices that worked for one secure channel type now also works for another.

questions: can ace use tls instead of dtls
what does rfc 9430 change in rfc 9202
dtls or tls for ace clients
subtitle: A tiny update that says the ACE DTLS profile works over TLS too, so constrained devices can fall back to TCP.

tldr.problem: The ACE DTLS profile in RFC 9202 only names DTLS, but UDP can be blocked on the path between a Client and a Resource Server, so a Client may need to fall back to CoAP over TCP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9430 declares that the profile applies to TLS as well as DTLS by replacing 'DTLS' with 'DTLS/TLS' in RFC 9202, and it adds rules for which one a Client tries first.
tldr.outcome: The same access token and the same access rights work over either DTLS or TLS between a given Client and Resource Server. The coap_dtls profile name is unchanged.

facts.label: Constrained devices
facts.value: SHOULD support DTLS, MAY support TLS

facts.label: Nonconstrained devices
facts.value: SHOULD support both TLS and DTLS

facts.label: Transport pairing
facts.value: DTLS for UDP, TLS for TCP

today: RFC 9430 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2023. It updates RFC 9202 and has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: Why the DTLS Profile Needs TLS
sections.content:
The Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE) framework, RFC 9200, defines lightweight authentication between a Client, a Resource Server (RS) and an Authorization Server (AS). The Client and RS may be constrained devices. RFC 9202 specifies how DTLS provides transport layer security between the nodes, but it works equally well for TLS.

Constrained implementations usually prefer CoAP over UDP. When ACE is deployed in networks run by other parties, such as the Internet, UDP might be blocked between the Client and the RS. The Client may then have to fall back to CoAP over TCP for NAT or firewall traversal. The OSCORE profile (RFC 9203) already supports both.
sections.plainLanguage: Small gadgets like to send short notes by one route. If a guard blocks that route, they need a second route that also stays private.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 9202
sections.content:
RFC 9430 updates RFC 9202 by specifying that the profile applies to TLS as well as DTLS. It only affects the transport layer security channel between the Client and the Resource Server. The same access rights are valid whether DTLS or TLS is used, and the same access token can be used by either between a given Client and RS pair.

The main change is to replace 'DTLS' with 'DTLS/TLS' throughout RFC 9202. This mostly affects the use of secure transport described in Sections 3.2.2, 3.3.2, 4 and 5 of that document. As a result, the value coap_dtls in the ace_profile parameter of an AS-to-Client response, or in the ace_profile claim of an access token, now means that either DTLS or TLS can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook said 'use road A'. The new one says 'road A or road B', and the same ticket works on both.

sections.title: Connection Establishment
sections.content:
A Client still follows RFC 9202 to get an access token from an Authorization Server and set up a security association with a specific Resource Server. The ace_profile parameter in the Client-to-AS request and the AS-to-Client response says which ACE profile the Client uses with the RS.

Because the parameter indicates the DTLS profile, the Client typically tries DTLS first. If that fails, the Client MAY try TLS to reach the Resource Server.

Constrained devices are not expected to support both mechanisms, so Clients and Resource Servers SHOULD support DTLS and MAY support TLS. A Client that implements only one of them might fail to establish a secure channel at all. Nonconstrained Clients and Resource Servers SHOULD support both.
sections.plainLanguage: Small gadgets try the usual road first and only switch to the other road if the first one fails. Big computers should know both roads.

sections.title: Choosing the Transport for the First Request
sections.content:
When a Client does not know a Resource Server in advance, it typically sends an initial unauthorized resource request, as illustrated in Section 2 of RFC 9202. If that exchange succeeds, the Client SHOULD use the same underlying transport protocol to set up the security association: DTLS for UDP, and TLS for TCP.

So the transport used for the first request also depends on what the Client supports. A Client that supports either DTLS or TLS but not both SHOULD use the transport protocol underneath the mechanism it supports for that initial request.
sections.plainLanguage: If you knock on the door using one road, you keep using the same road to go inside. A gadget that knows only one road starts on that road.

sections.title: IANA Registry Change
sections.content: In the 'ACE Profiles' registry, the Description and Reference fields for coap_dtls have been updated. The name and the CBOR value (1) stay the same. The description now says the profile delegates client authentication and authorization by establishing a DTLS or TLS channel between resource-constrained nodes, and the reference lists RFC 9202 and RFC 9430.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names kept the same entry, but its description was edited to say it covers both roads.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document adds no new security text of its own. It states that the security considerations and requirements of RFC 9202, TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and BCP 195 (RFC 8996 and RFC 9325) also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules from before still apply. Nothing new was added, so the old rules cover both roads.
